transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees (Redwood): Alex Navarro, Priya Desai, Marcus Li
Attendees (Customer): Lena Ortiz, Tom Blake, Maya Chen, Ravi Patel

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Redwood and Seraphim ran a QBR-style health sync focused on runway for service rollout, cost tradeoffs across hosted/dedicated/private, and operational playbooks for canary rollouts. Customer emphasized latency SLOs for checkout flows and strict audit logging requirements. Agreed next steps: pricing spreadsheet, perf tests, compliance doc checklist, and pilot timeline.

Topics: 
- Usage/consumption trajectory and forecasting
- Cost per model/variant and quantization options
- Latency SLOs and canary/fallback policies
- Security/compliance (SOC 2, SSO, encryption/KMS)
- Pilot scope and rollout playbook

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Navarro: Alright, thanks everyone for joining. Uh, this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Today we're going to... try to walk through runway and the model rollout playbook, figure out the pilot items and cost buckets. How does that sound, Lena?
[00:08] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good, thanks Alex. We want to be practical — checkout latency is our primary KPI, and finance is watching unit economics as the storefront goes live.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Yep, short intro from finance — we need predictability. If there are big token surges, we need a committed runway or we'll have trouble forecasting spend.
[00:24] Alex Navarro: Right, so we'll cover hosted vs Dedicated capacity and then Private deployment constraints. Priya will jump into perf considerations.
[00:30] Priya Desai: Hi everyone — I'll focus on throughput/latency and the canary plan, and Marcus will cover model variants and rollback strategy.
[00:36] Tom Blake: Quick one — our infra team is mostly AWS, VPC peered to our app VPC. We are open to both Redwood Dedicated and Private; it comes down to cost and how fast we can get an SLA.
[00:46] Marcus Li: Important thing to call out — Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so tail latency is predictable under commit. Private gives you control over networking and keys, but requires extra provisioning lead time.
[00:58] Ravi Patel: From security, we need audit logs, KMS integration, and for any private deployment we need SSO/SAML and RBAC mapping to our IdP. Also some customers call for data residency so we need region constraints.
[01:11] Priya Desai: Understood. We support KMS and HSM integrations for Private, and for Dedicated we offer tenant-level encryption keys. Audit logs and token-level tracing are available in the Redwood Console out of the box — we'll show sample retention and routing.
[01:25] Lena Ortiz: Great. On latency — our checkout flow target is p95 under 250ms for generative recommendation calls, and p99 closer to 400ms. Is that in scope?
[01:34] Alex Navarro: Yes, that's reasonable. For hosted models we typically recommend a model variant tuned for latency — e.g., smaller quantized model on Dedicated gives you better p95 for that percentile. Priya, can you walk through the numbers we saw in the benchmark doc?
[01:46] Priya Desai: Sure — quick numbers off memory: on T4-equivalent Dedicated we saw p95 around 180-220ms for the x-lite quantized variant at batch size 8 and sequence len 64. On the full fp16 variant p95 jumped to ~320ms. So there's a clear tradeoff. Also, cold-start can add 200–400ms if KV cache hasn't warmed.
[02:09] Tom Blake: Cold start is our nightmare during flash sales. How do you handle cache warmup and burst?
[02:14] Priya Desai: We recommend a small steady warmup traffic and then a burst buffer — Redwood's automatic prefix caching and continuous batching reduce token cost and help the warm start. For big bursts we have burst capacity configs on Dedicated to spin up more workers quickly — depends on the commit level.
[02:29] Lena Ortiz: And pricing — can you show ballpark per-1M token numbers for the variants?
[02:34] Alex Navarro: We'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet, but high level: hosted latency-optimized variants are more expensive per token; Dedicated with a commit reduces unit cost significantly — like 30–55% depending on utilization and quantization. Private is highest upfront but can lower long-run TCO if you amortize infra. We'll share the matrix.
[02:50] Maya Chen: Important — can you show the math for our 3x expected traffic growth? We need scenario analysis.
[02:56] Marcus Li: Yep, we'll include three scenarios: base, +2x, +5x. The perf test plan Priya creates will run scaled traffic so you can validate.
[03:05] Ravi Patel: On compliance — SOC 2 is required for our auditors; do you have an attestation? Also, we need to know about log retention windows and whether logs can be exported to our S3.
[03:15] Alex Navarro: We have SOC 2 Type II — we'll share the cert and a redacted version of the control matrix. Logs can be exported; for Private we can push directly to your S3 or SIEM, for Dedicated you can configure retention via the console and export hooks.
[03:27] Tom Blake: Network-wise, we need to see the VPC peering diagram and egress patterns. We can't have any unexpected cross-tenant egress.
[03:34] Priya Desai: We'll share a diagram. For Dedicated there's no cross-tenant network egress; Private gives you the most control. If you need air-gapped we'll outline the on-prem options but that has longer lead times.
[03:46] Lena Ortiz: Let's talk about rollout strategy — we want a canary for 10% of checkout traffic, metric-driven, auto-roll back on latency or error spike.
[03:55] Marcus Li: Recommended playbook: 1) Canary to 5–10% with shadowing for 30 minutes, 2) monitor latency and correctness via synthetic prompts and production traffic, 3) expand to 50% with autoscale policy on Dedicated, 4) full cutover. We'll provide the canary thresholds and a rollback playbook.
[04:14] Priya Desai: Also include a fail-open policy where if Redwood experiences capacity issues we can fallback to a smaller model or a cached response path — we can automate that via routing policy.
[04:24] Tom Blake: Ok but we need to ensure the fallback doesn't leak PII or change billing semantics.
[04:29] Alex Navarro: Good point — we'll make sure fallback path follows the same redaction/PII rules and we can scope it to non-sensitive prompts, or return cached generic answers. We'll document billing differences.
[04:39] Lena Ortiz: For the pilot timeline — we're aiming to be live on a beta path in mid-June. Is that feasible?
[04:45] Alex Navarro: Feasible if we get sprint alignment this week: Redwood delivers pricing and perf plan by 5/25, perf test week of 5/31, and then a short integration sprint. Marcus, any infra lead time constraints?
[04:58] Marcus Li: For Dedicated we can spin up reserved pools within 7–10 business days after contract and capacity commitments. Private needs networking and KMS setup — usually 3–4 weeks. If timeline is mid-June, Dedicated is the more likely path.
[05:12] Maya Chen: Finance leaning to Dedicated if it clears the unit economics — less operational burden than Private for a first pilot.
[05:18] Priya Desai: We'll include quantized vs fp16 cost/latency lines and a recommendation matrix by workload. For recommendation-type prompts with short output we usually pick x-lite quantized.
[05:29] Ravi Patel: One small ask — can you provide an example audit trail for a single request including token-level cost attribution? Our compliance team wants to see traceability.
[05:38] Alex Navarro: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level attribution and you can export per-request traces. We'll attach a screenshot and a sample CSV in the follow-up.
[05:46] Lena Ortiz: Any gotchas we should be aware of?
[05:49] Priya Desai: A couple: 1) Measuring latency end-to-end requires including network hops — so measure from your app to the model entrypoint, 2) prompt engineering can reduce token costs dramatically by constraining output length, and 3) quantization reduces latency and cost but sometimes slightly affects quality — we'll run evals against your prompt sets.
[06:07] Tom Blake: For the perf test, can Redwood simulate our real auth layer? We use signed JWTs and a bastion flow.
[06:14] Marcus Li: We can run tests behind a staging proxy that mirrors your auth. We'll need a short runbook and a service account and some sample tokens.
[06:23] Lena Ortiz: Great. Anything on SSO mapping and RBAC for the Redwood Console?
[06:27] Alex Navarro: We support SAML SSO and can map roles to your IdP groups. For Dedicated/Private we can pre-provision accounts and assign roles via the console API.
[06:37] Maya Chen: Finance question — are there minimum commitment tiers for Dedicated that would affect our runway?
[06:42] Alex Navarro: Yes, Dedicated has monthly commits that get you lower per-token rates. We'll include an amortization example in the pricing sheet.
[06:49] Ravi Patel: Also note that our legal needs a data processing addendum — who on Redwood Legal can own that?
[06:55] Alex Navarro: I'll loop in our contracts lead, Sarah Kim, after the call. She usually handles DPAs and enterprise addenda.
[07:03] Lena Ortiz: Anything else? If not let's recap next steps.
[07:06] Alex Navarro: Quick recap: Redwood action items — pricing matrix (Alex), perf test plan (Priya), canary/rollback playbook (Marcus), SOC2 and audit artifacts (Alex + legal). Customer action items — share prompt sets and traffic histograms (Lena), provide list of compliance questions (Ravi), confirm pilot SLOs and preferred deployment mode (Tom/Maya).
[07:27] Tom Blake: I'll coordinate the staging tokens and network diagram with Priya.
[07:31] Maya Chen: We'll review the pricing and aim to sign commitments if the numbers align.
[07:36] Alex Navarro: Great — we'll aim to get the materials out by Tuesday the 25th. Thanks everyone.
[07:41] Lena Ortiz: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
